paragraphs: Worth trying first: willing to stand for long periods at a fixed workstation, measure and mark repeatedly and cut by hand according to work orders and templates, able to accept repetitive motions and dimensional tolerance requirements, willing to wear protective equipment as specified, maintain cutting tools and pick out defective items against inspection standards, and willing to stop and report upward when a tool behaves abnormally, material is defective or a part is out of tolerance.

Consider carefully: if you find it hard to stand for long periods and repeat the same motions, are sensitive to dusty and noisy environments, are unwilling to verify strictly against dimensions and templates, or find repeated inspection and packing tedious, the actual work will differ from your expectations.

The core output is finished parts that meet specification and can be verified, together with records: pieces cut to dimensions and templates, finished items trimmed and sanded properly, inspection and defect marking records, counting or weighing and bundling results, and tool and equipment maintenance records — not "how many cuts you made".

Low-risk validation: using safe materials such as cardboard, fabric or foam, complete one exercise — "read the dimensions from a fictional work order — mark and position using a template — cut along the line — measure to check whether the tolerance is exceeded — pick out and mark defects — count and pack" — this only assesses work preferences; the exercise uses no dangerous equipment other than cutting tools and does not involve real production orders or client data, and is not equivalent to employer hiring or authorization to work.

Judgment focus: whether, under the constraints of work order dimensions, template tolerances and safety procedures, you can turn measuring and marking, cutting and profiling, trimming and sanding, and inspection and packing into finished items and records that are verifiable, transferable and traceable.

Work pace is determined by order batch size and delivery dates, material type and thickness, and the frequency of die and template changes; across settings such as manufacturing lines, manual workshops and processing shops, product types, equipment and inspection standards differ markedly.

Similar job titles among adjacent occupations do not mean the same duties; when comparing, first look at whether the focus is manual cutting and trimming, cutting and slicing machine operation, metal punching and shearing equipment operation, hand grinding and polishing, or machine feeding and offbearing, and whether the role carries equipment operation, die adjustment or quality release responsibility.

Work orders, templates, measuring tools and inspection standards may be treated as inputs that must be followed, but you must not skip measuring and first-piece verification based on experience, nor substitute visual judgment for the required checks on dimensions, burrs, scratches and colour differences.
A fit assessment should be checked against real work observation, mentoring feedback and your own condition; it cannot be replaced by an interest type or a single test.

All paper exercises on this page use fictional materials; in real production, tool and equipment operation, personal protection, dust and noise protection, and material and finished goods inspection must follow safety procedures, position work instructions and employer policies.

Hand cutters and trimmers work with manufactured materials that need cutting and trimming, including carpet, fabric, stone, glass and rubber, along with work orders, templates, measuring tools and inspection standards; the outputs are pieces and finished items that meet dimensional and appearance specifications, defect markings and inspection results, counting, weighing and packing records, and tool and equipment maintenance records; the basis for handling is work order dimensions and tolerances, template and measuring tool readings, position work instructions, safety and protection procedures, and the employer's inspection and escalation paths — not the job title.

The work of hand cutters and trimmers can be divided into three connected but distinct work areas. The first is cutting to work order and profiling: reading the work order to determine dimensions, cutting positions and quantities, positioning and marking on the material using templates, measuring tools or a straightedge; cutting and profiling with hand tools, shears, hand-held power tools or bench cutting equipment; cutting openings or notches as needed; and adjusting guides and stops to control cutting depth and width. The second is trimming and sanding: removing excess edge material and loose threads, pressing bench cutting tools down to the specified specification, folding or shaping the material before and after cutting, replacing or sharpening blunt tools and blades, and then using grinding wheels, brushes and cleaning and polishing materials to sand, polish and clean the finished item. The third is inspection and packing: picking out defects such as spots, stains, scratches, chipped corners and unacceptable shapes and marking them for scrap; separating and grading by size, weight, type, condition, colour or colour difference; marking the finished item with a number, trademark, grade, size or model; counting or weighing and then bundling and stacking; and using a cart to move the pieces to the next process or the storage area. The three work areas alternate, but their basis, tolerances and risks differ; so do the materials, equipment and inspection standards across settings such as line production, small order batches and manual workshops.

Where are the boundaries between hand cutters and trimmers and adjacent machine cutting, hand grinding and feeding positions?

When comparing manual cutting and trimming, machine cutting and slicing, hand grinding and polishing, machine feeding and offbearing, and textile cutting, verify by the main tasks and the mode of equipment operation. The tasks overlap: this occupation also lists bench tools and guide adjustment, and feeders also inspect and record; it cannot be inferred from the names that there is no inspection, no equipment adjustment, or final release authority.
Core purpose

Use hand tools or hand-held power tools to cut, trim and sand finished products such as carpet, fabric, stone, glass and rubber to work order and template, so that dimensions and appearance meet specification.

Core purposes of adjacent occupations: cutting and slicing machine setters, operators and tenders set up and tend cutting or slicing machines to complete batch cutting; grinding and polishing workers, hand, use hand tools and hand-held power tools to grind and polish workpiece surfaces; machine feeders and offbearers feed machines or remove machined parts from them; textile cutting machine setters, operators and tenders operate textile cutting machines to cut pieces in batches to patterns.
Main objects and basis

Manufactured materials that need cutting and trimming, work order dimensions and tolerances, templates and measuring tools; the basis is work instructions, inspection standards, safety and protection procedures, and the employer's review and escalation paths.

Adjacent objects: cutting and slicing equipment and work order settings (51-9032), parts awaiting grinding and polishing and surface requirements (51-9022), machine feeding and offbearing and material state (53-7063), multilayer fabric and templates and cutting equipment (51-6062); these tasks overlap with manual handling and inspection.
Core process
Read the work order → measure and mark → cut and profile → trim and sand → inspect and mark → count, pack and move.

Processes of adjacent occupations: clamp the material and set machine parameters and then tend the run (cutting and slicing machine setters, operators and tenders), grind and polish piece by piece to the surface requirements (grinding and polishing workers, hand), feed the machine or remove finished items to the takt (machine feeders and offbearers), and cut multiple pieces at once on a cutting machine to a pattern (textile cutting machine setters, operators and tenders).
Main outputs
Pieces and finished items that meet specification, defect markings and inspection results, counting, weighing and packing records, tool and equipment maintenance records.

Outputs of adjacent occupations: batches of cut pieces and machine parameter records (cutting and slicing machine setters, operators and tenders), polished parts that meet surface requirements (grinding and polishing workers, hand), stable work-in-progress flow and loading/unloading records (machine feeders and offbearers), and pattern-cut pieces and marker records (textile cutting machine setters, operators and tenders).
Responsible party

Staff in this occupation are responsible for the dimensions, appearance and inspection results of the parts they process; tool replacement, equipment maintenance and stopping the line to report an out-of-tolerance condition must follow the work instructions and employer procedures, not their unilateral decision.

Editorial check suggestion: verify the actual position responsible for each item of machine parameters, processing quality, material state and cut piece specifications; occupational profiles list tasks and cannot be used to infer an individual's final release, safety sign-off or modification authority.
Collaboration and supervision

Collaborate with workers in the same process, inspectors, team leaders and equipment maintenance within the scope of authority, and report to a supervisor or along the review path; when a tool behaves abnormally, material is defective, equipment fails or a part is out of tolerance, stop processing and report, refer and keep records according to procedure.

Collaboration of adjacent occupations: cutting and slicing machine operators collaborate with setup and inspection staff; grinding and polishing workers collaborate with inspection and the next process; machine feeders and offbearers collaborate with machine operators; textile cutting machine operators collaborate with pattern-making and sewing processes.
Boundary of conclusions

Similar names do not mean the same duties; hand-held and bench tools overlap, so equipment setup, dies, material flow, inspection and maintenance authority must be verified against the actual position, and final release authority cannot be inferred from the occupation title.

The preparation levels and equipment operation requirements of adjacent occupations do not apply to this occupation; verify them item by item against each occupation's official materials and the requirements of the position.
Key occupational judgments

Six recurring professional judgments: whether the work order dimensions, quantities and cutting positions are read correctly; whether the template and measuring tool positioning is accurate and the marking clear; whether the cutting and profiling are within tolerance and the guides and stops are set correctly; whether excess material, loose threads and burrs are removed cleanly and the sanding and polishing meet the surface requirements; whether defects are picked out and marked truthfully and the separation and grading match the inspection standards; and whether, when a tool behaves abnormally, material is defective, equipment fails or a part is out of tolerance, the machine is stopped, the item isolated and the matter escalated first.
Determine the dimensions, cutting positions and quantities from the work order and verify the material and batch; misreading leads to a whole batch of pieces being scrapped or excess consumption.
Position using templates, measuring tools and a straightedge and mark the cutting line clearly on the material; positioning deviation goes straight into the cut result.
Cut and profile to specification and adjust the guides and stops; exceeding tolerance causes rework, scrap and assembly problems.

Remove excess material and loose threads cleanly, press the tool down to the specified dimension and sand and polish to the surface requirements; an unacceptable surface affects the appearance and acceptance of the finished item.
Judgment four: Do the trimming and sanding meet the requirements?

Pick out defects such as spots, scratches and chipped corners against the inspection standards and mark, separate and grade them truthfully; missed defects flow into the next process and trigger complaints.
Judgment five: Are the defects and grading consistent?
When a tool behaves abnormally, material is defective, equipment fails or a part is out of tolerance, stop the machine, isolate the item and report upward according to procedure, keeping records.

Work context and working conditions

U.S. respondent work context indicates prolonged standing and repetitive hand operations; different materials, tools and workstations involve different exposures, and not all positions can be generalized as daily contact with dust and noise.

Among O*NET respondents, 91% reported working indoors under controlled environmental conditions every day and 80% reported standing continually or almost continually. A further 28% reported daily contact with contaminants (including gases, dust and odours) and 22% daily contact with distracting or uncomfortable noise; the corresponding frequencies are not exposure doses, exceedances of hazard limits or disease rates.

The objects are finished products such as carpet, fabric, stone, glass and rubber; the task profile also lists food ingredients and metal. Hand tools, hand-held power tools or some bench tools may be used, and the occupation must not be merged into the 51-9032 machine cutting occupation merely because of bench equipment. Measuring tools, templates, abrasives and handling methods are verified against the actual process; Excel, Outlook and Word are listed only on the hot technology posting text page and do not prove on-site use.

Then measure and mark in order, cut and profile, trim and sand, inspect and mark, and after counting or weighing bundle, stack and hand over to the next process; before handover, organize unfinished pieces and pending items and hand over according to procedure; when a tool behaves abnormally, material is defective, equipment fails or a part is out of tolerance, stop processing and report upward according to procedure.

Among O*NET respondents, 96% reported a typical 40-hour week, 80% standing continually or almost continually, 43% repetitive motions continually or almost continually (a further 35% more than half the time), and 20% facing strict deadlines once or more a week but not every day. Each item is the distribution of a different question and cannot be used to derive Chinese working hours or peak-season overtime rates.

Report to a supervisor or along the review path; current O*NET profile (51-9031.00; page updated 2026, not a unified survey year): 56% rated "continual contact with others" as the highest level, 22% rated collaboration with a team as extremely important and 36% rated coordinating or leading others as extremely important, 39% described their freedom in determining tasks and priorities as very great, and 38% described decision freedom as "some".

The profile supports tasks of dimensions, defects, tools and marking; first-piece checks, sampling, records, out-of-tolerance isolation and reporting paths are verification suggestions designed for this page from the tasks and are determined by employer procedures, not a system directly prescribed by the O*NET survey.

O*NET currently lists 12 work styles, the higher ones being attention to detail 80, dependability 67 and caution 59; these are Impact scores, not population percentages or personality test thresholds. Actual safety measures are determined by material, equipment and risk assessment; work context cannot replace a health assessment.

Cutting, Punching, and Press Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic

paragraphs: Cutting and Slicing Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders (adjacent occupation, 51-9032.00)
Set up and tend cutting or slicing machines to cut material continuously into slices, blocks or strips to specification, monitoring the run and the output.

The difference is that the core is a fixed machine and batch parameters, and the objects are the machine's cutting tools and feed; this occupation centers on cutting and trimming with hand and hand-held tools, with machines being only one kind of tool.
Better suited to people who want to do machine setup and batch monitoring.
Cutting, Punching, and Press Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic (adjacent occupation, 51-4031.00)
Set up and operate punching, shearing or press equipment to punch, cut and form metal or plastic.

The difference is that the objects are metal and plastic sheet and forming relies on punching dies; this occupation mostly works with finished products such as carpet, fabric, stone, glass and rubber.
Better suited to people who want to work with punching dies and metal processing.
Grinding and Polishing Workers, Hand (adjacent occupation, 51-9022.00)

The difference is that the core is surface treatment and the role is not responsible for cutting to size and profiling; this occupation centers on cutting to size and trimming, with sanding only a finishing step.
Better suited to people who want to specialize in surface sanding and polishing.
Machine Feeders and Offbearers (adjacent occupation, 53-7063.00)

The difference is that they do not set process parameters and are not responsible for the dimensions and appearance of the finished product; this occupation must be responsible for the dimensions and appearance of the parts it processes.
Better suited to people who want to do loading, unloading and material flow work.
Textile Cutting Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders (adjacent occupation, 51-6062.00)
The difference is that the core is pattern marking and multilayer cutting in large batches; this occupation relies more on single-piece measuring, marking and manual trimming.
Better suited to people who want to do pattern marking and batch piece cutting.
Molders, Shapers, and Casters, Except Metal and Plastic (adjacent occupation, 51-9195.00)
The difference is that the core is forming and casting, which changes the form of the material; this occupation mainly cuts and trims a given material to size.
Better suited to people who want to do forming processes and dies.

values: Fictional production scenario material (exercise input)

Fictional scenario: a hand cutter and trimmer encounters four problems during a shift. First, a batch of material has local scratches and colour differences, and the appearance grade required by the work order is unclear; second, a measured piece sits at the edge of the tolerance and it is unclear whether it can be released; third, after the bench cutting tool is pressed down there is burring and the tool is somewhat blunt; fourth, the delivery date is very tight and the team leader wants to finish the work first and add the first-piece record afterwards.

Materials provided: work order dimensions and quantities; appearance grades and defect limit samples; inspection and first-piece confirmation requirements; tool maintenance and replacement procedures.

Materials not provided: the rules for judging and conceding edge dimensions, the authority to perform tool replacement, the order of first-piece records, and the division of responsibility for deviation and missed defects. If the exercise requires these conditions, state your assumptions and the people you need to confirm with.
Task requirements

Please write a one-page handling and reporting plan covering: verification and handling recommendations for defects and colour differences, re-verification and handling of edge dimensions, handling of burring and tool problems, and the order of first-piece checks and records under delivery pressure.
The plan must state which information comes from the given materials and which is still assumption, and indicate whether the basis is the work order, inspection standards or tool procedures.
Reference deliverable (can be derived from the prompt)

The plan should include: defects and colour differences (verify piece by piece against the limit samples, pick out and mark items beyond the limit, and ask inspection or the team leader to confirm when uncertain rather than relaxing the standard yourself), edge dimensions (re-measure and verify whether they are within tolerance, stop the machine and isolate and report according to procedure on deviation, and do not release on your own), burring and tools (replace or sharpen the tool according to procedure and re-set and confirm the first piece before continuing), delivery pressure (explain that the first-piece check and records cannot be omitted, and apply for an adjustment or additional resources when necessary rather than finishing first and recording later), and handover (state the status of the four items, the actions taken and the matters still to be confirmed).
The reference deliverable only lists the elements that should be included and does not require wording identical to the example; being able to explain the basis for your judgements is enough.

This item only tests awareness of dimensional verification, inspection judgement, tool and safety handling and anomaly escalation; it does not evaluate whether the handling of any real case is compliant, and it does not constitute a safety determination, liability determination or legal advice.

Do not use real production orders or unredacted commercial information; where real tool and equipment operation, personal protection, dust and noise protection and finished goods inspection are involved, safety procedures, work instructions and unit policies must be followed.

entries.answer: Use hand tools or hand-held power tools to cut and trim finished products such as carpet, fabric, stone, glass and rubber: read the work order to determine dimensions, cutting positions and quantities; position using templates or measuring tools and mark cutting lines on the material; cut, form and trim the material with hand tools, shears, hand-held power tools or bench cutting equipment; adjust guides and stops to control cutting depth and width; separate materials by size, weight, type, condition, colour or colour difference; fold or shape before and after cutting; remove excess material and loose threads and press bench cutting tools down to the specified specification; replace or sharpen blunt tools and blades; sand, polish, clean and mark the finished item (number, trademark, grade, size or model); pick out and mark defects such as spots, stains, scratches, chipped corners and unacceptable shapes; and count or weigh before bundling, stacking and moving to the next process or storage area by cart.
entries.question: What does the daily work of a hand cutter and trimmer involve?

entries.answer: This occupation mainly cuts, trims and sands finished products by hand and with hand-held tools to work orders and templates and must be responsible for the dimensions and appearance of the parts it processes; cutting and slicing machine setters, operators and tenders centre on fixed machine setup and batch monitoring; cutting, punching and press machine setters, operators and tenders, metal and plastic, centre on punching dies and metal and plastic sheet processing; grinding and polishing workers, hand, centre on surface treatment and are not responsible for cutting to size; machine feeders and offbearers are only responsible for feeding the line and do not set process parameters or inspection results; textile cutting machine setters, operators and tenders centre on pattern marking and multilayer cutting; molders, shapers and casters, except metal and plastic, centre on forming and casting to change the form of the material. Similar names do not mean duties or equipment operation requirements can be swapped.

description.text: Cutters and Trimmers, Hand (O*NET-SOC 51-9031.00) use hand tools or hand-held power tools to cut and trim finished products such as carpet, fabric, stone, glass and rubber: covering reading the work order to determine dimensions and quantities, marking and positioning to template or measuring tool, cutting and profiling with cutting tools and shears or bench cutting equipment, separating materials by size, weight, type and colour, folding and shaping, trimming excess material and loose threads, adjusting guides and stops, replacing and sharpening tools, sanding, polishing, cleaning and marking the finished item, and counting, weighing, packing and moving; it should be noted that its U.S. wage and employment follow this subcategory's own basis (2025 median annual wage 38,020 dollars, hourly 18.28 dollars; about 7,000 people employed in 2024; a 2024—2034 projection of a decline of -1% or lower; about 600 annual average openings including growth and replacement; industry distribution manufacturing 70% | other industries 30%; interest code RC), together with the industry-level gap for such positions in mainland China and control points for tool safety, hand protection, dimensional verification and quality inspection.

subject.name: Cutters and Trimmers, Hand
subject.summary: In the United States, cutters and trimmers, hand, correspond to O*NET-SOC 51-9031.00 (Cutters and Trimmers, Hand), using hand tools or hand-held power tools to cut and trim finished products such as carpet, fabric, stone, glass and rubber: reading the work order to determine dimensions, cutting positions and quantities, positioning to template or measuring tool and marking on the material; cutting to order and profiling with hand cutting tools, shears, hand-held power tools or bench cutting equipment; separating materials by size, weight, type, colour or colour difference, and folding or shaping before and after cutting; trimming excess material and loose threads and pressing bench cutting tools down to the specified specification; adjusting guides and stops to control cutting depth and width; replacing or sharpening blunt tools and blades; sanding, polishing, cleaning and marking the finished item, and counting or weighing before bundling, stacking and moving to the next process. The preparation level for this occupation is Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation, SVP below 6.0), typically requiring a high school diploma or equivalent with some positions requiring none, and on-the-job training ranging from a few days to a year. Comparable positions in China are manual cutting, trimming and sanding positions in manufacturing and processing enterprises; their duties and pay basis do not correspond one-to-one with this U.S. occupational subcategory and cannot be interchanged.
